title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and her advisor discuss a research project on multimodal AI models.

script.en: Professor, I've been reading about multimodal foundation models that combine vision and language. The claims are impressive, but I'm not sure how much these systems actually understand.

That's a crucial question. Many models appear fluent because they've been trained on massive datasets, but their apparent competence often masks serious gaps in reasoning. What specifically concerns you?
Well, I tried a popular model with a simple task: identifying an object in an image after seeing just one example. It failed completely, even though it could describe the image in elaborate detail.
Exactly. That's a classic case of superficial fluency. The model learns statistical associations, not grounded concepts. Our lab has been developing benchmarks to expose these failures.
So how do you get models to learn without huge annotated datasets? I mean, annotation is expensive and time-consuming.

We use techniques like contrastive learning, where the model sees matching and mismatching pairs of audio and images. It learns to align representations without explicit labels. We also mask parts of the input and ask the model to reconstruct them.
That sounds like how children learn—by associating what they see with what they hear. But do these methods really lead to deeper understanding?
They help, but they're not a cure-all. The key is to design benchmarks that test genuine understanding, not just pattern matching. Then we can measure progress honestly.
I see. So the goal isn't just to build bigger models, but to make them more reliable and transparent.
Precisely. And that needs collaboration between vision, speech, and language experts. It's a long road, but we're making steady progress.

script.en: In recent years, artificial intelligence has made great progress in handling many kinds of data at once. Systems can now analyze images, audio, and text together, and such systems are common in research labs and tech companies. However, more and more experts warn that these systems often lack true understanding. They may still produce fluent descriptions or answer questions correctly, and for example, a model might describe a scene in detail. Yet it may fail to locate a specific object when given only a few examples. This shows a troubling gap between appearance and reality, and this gap has led researchers to develop new ways to evaluate such systems. Benchmarks are being designed to test whether models truly understand links between different modalities. The goal is to see if they do more than just memorize patterns. At the same time, scientists are exploring training methods that rely less on large labeled datasets. Methods such as contrastive learning show real promise, and in this approach, models learn from matching and mismatching pairs. By masking parts of the input and requiring reconstruction, models can build stronger internal representations. These representations support deeper generalization, and yet experts caution that no single method is a cure-all. The final goal is to build systems that are not only powerful but also transparent and reliable. This needs lasting teamwork across fields, from computer vision to linguistics, and as one researcher puts it, the journey is long. But each step brings us closer to machines that interact with the world more like humans do.

sections.title: Multimodal AI: Fluency vs. Understanding
sections.passage: Multimodal foundation models combine vision, audio, and language into one framework, and they have made great progress in recent years. They can now do many tasks that were once thought extremely difficult. They can describe images in detail, transcribe speech accurately, and answer complex questions with ease. This often gives the impression that they deeply understand the content they process. Yet a closer look reveals a troubling gap, and their fluent output often hides a shallow understanding of basic concepts. This gap between surface performance and real understanding has become a central concern for researchers. Researchers at MIT and IBM have been studying these failures, and they are developing methods to overcome them. The goal is to build systems whose competence is based on real understanding, not just surface pattern matching. One major issue is that top models often fail at tasks that need grounding. Grounding means linking words to specific objects or events in the real world. For example, a model like GPT-4o may fail to locate a particular object in an image after seeing just a few examples. This happens even though it can produce elaborate descriptions that sound very convincing. Such failures suggest that the models rely on statistical patterns rather than genuine understanding. They also raise serious questions about how far current systems can be trusted in practical use. To address this, the team created benchmarks that expose these weaknesses, and these benchmarks allow honest evaluation. Progress can then be measured against meaningful criteria, not just impressive but misleading demonstrations, and another challenge is the heavy reliance on annotated training data. This has long been a bottleneck in multimodal research, and creating large-scale annotations is expensive and time-consuming. It often limits the diversity of data that can be used, and the researchers therefore explored data-efficient techniques, such as contrastive learning. In contrastive learning, the model learns from matching and mismatching pairs of inputs. By aligning representations without explicit labels, the model can build more robust internal knowledge, and this knowledge generalizes better to new situations. In addition, masking parts of the input and requiring reconstruction helps the model build stronger links between modalities. This lets it infer missing information and connect visual, auditory, and linguistic cues more effectively. However, these techniques are not a cure-all, and the researchers are careful to acknowledge their limitations. The team stresses that the goal is not just to build larger models. The goal is to make them more transparent and reliable, so their behavior can be understood and predicted. This requires sustained collaboration across disciplines, from speech and vision to language processing, and it also requires a willingness to confront uncomfortable findings. As one researcher notes, the journey is long, but steady progress is being made. In the end, the pursuit of human-like interaction in AI demands more than superficial fluency.

long_sentences.en: We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data.

An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision.

A: When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language.
